strengths: Some of the problems identified in this work seem convincing -- the use of only two outputs, and the problem of decreasing likelihood of preferred responses.
Results show improvement compared to baselines on mt-bench and alpaca-eval.
An analysis shows regularization in SPO-abs is effective, indeed the prob. of the preferred response does not decrease anymore.
The paper studies a generalization of the DPO objective to the multiclass setting, which could be a more efficient way to train models when there are multiple generations per prompt.
The paper evaluates the performance of the proposed objectives across multiple settings.

The paper clearly specifies its goal to devise an algorithm that learns from both preference labels as well as pointwise scalar rewards, that are both typically found in popular preference alignment from human feedback datasets. The benchmarks and baselines chosen are relevant and reasonable.
weaknesses: The authors claim that using a list of rewards is more efficient and convenient than using preferences, which runs counter to past work; they do not argue for this approach or state it as a limitation.
The authors seem not to acknowledge relevant past work on using soft labels instead of hard labels, such as the paper "robust preference optimization" by Fisch et al.

Prior work (e.g., Pal et al., Fisch et al., Liu et al.) addressing reducing likelihood is not properly discussed; the authors cite Pal et al. but omit mention of their positive-DPO variant and related papers.
There exists work on using lists of generations in alignment (LIRE) that is not cited.
Extending the binary case to multiclass without softness is incremental and fails to exploit full information in the list of generations, making the single-correct-class assumption problematic.
The statement of what the authors are trying to solve is unclear (multiple responses, scalar rewards, likelihood ratio decrease of DPO, etc.).
The related work paragraph unnecessarily goes back to BERT and distracts from the flow.

The motivation for choosing the reasoning setup is unclear; it is uncertain whether SPO will be good for this setup, and there is a mismatch between the dataset used for training the reward model and the benchmarks used for evaluation, making results hard to interpret.
The phrasing "dark knowledge" in "The soft label represents the important dark knowledge from the teacher LLM" should be rephrased.
The acronym LPO is used instead of SPO in the figures, likely a mistake.

The generalization of DPO to the multiclass setting is not evaluated sufficiently on its own; it is unclear whether to use the multiclass objective or a binary objective over pairs of generations, and computational efficiency (memory usage) is not discussed.

The use of a soft target distribution from a teacher model versus a hard target distribution has been proposed by prior work (e.g., Distilled DPO by Fisch et al. 2024) but is not discussed; the novelty claim is misleading, and the comparison is confounded because the teacher model is larger than the student model.

The additional objective in SPO-abs lacks contextualization in prior work; its hypothesis mirrors that of prior work (Pal et al. 2024), the formulation is not well motivated, the connection to NCE is underdeveloped, and it is unclear why prior approaches would not be sufficient; empirical comparison is needed.
Claims that SPO-abs can guarantee convergence to the optimal LM policy are not clearly supported or explained.
The paper would greatly benefit from a revision that more clearly establishes connections to prior work and disentangles the impact of the various aspects of the proposed methods.
The focus solely on the offline setting and the limited model scales explored in experiments are reasonable given expense, but may be seen as a limitation.

The motivation for choosing a soft-label based knowledge-distillation approach is not clear and related work does not mention any KD-based or Plackett-Luce based works that the main contribution (eq.9) is based on.
There are many presentation issues, including typos, mislabeling in figures, and inconsistencies between prose and figures.
